results.title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?
results.description: Giulio Starace, Oliver Jaffe, Dane Sherburn, James Aung, Jun Shern Chan, Leon Maksin, Rachel Dias, Evan Mays, Benjamin Kinsella, Wyatt Thompson, Johannes Heidecke, Amelia Glaese, and Tejal Patwardhan. PaperBench: Evaluating AI’s ability to replicate AI research. arXiv preprint arXiv:2504.01848, 2025.
extra_snippets: An agent must go beyond understanding a paper’s conclusion to recover how the result was obtained, translate incomplete descriptions into executable procedures, operate specialized tools, diagnose failures, and determine whether the resulting evidence actually supports the claim. Existing reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, while cross-domain scientific benchmarks typically isolate only parts of the workflow (Starace et al., 2025; Siegel et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2026).

The tasks run in 10 domain-native scien-tific computing environments, including Ansys HFSS, Ansys Lumerical, Meep (Oskooi et al., 2010), PySCF/GPU4PySCF (Sun et al., 2026), ABACUS (Zhou et al., 2025), Quantum ESPRESSO (Giannozzi et al., 2009), AutoDock Vina (Eberhardt et al., 2021), Habitat (Savva et al., 2019), SimplerEnv (Li et al., 2025), and AI2-THOR (Kolve et al., 2017).

MLAgentBench and RE-Bench evaluate long-horizon machine-learning experimentation and research engineering, but their objectives are specified as task-level metric improvement rather than reproduction of published claims (Huang et al., 2023; Wijk et al., 2024). PaperBench and SA-Bench move toward paper-level evaluation through reproduction or semantic-alignment rubrics (Starace et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026).

results.title: ResearchClawBench: A Benchmark for End-to-End Autonomous Scientific Research
results.description: ScienceAgentBench (Chen et al., 2025) extracts data-driven scientific discovery tasks from peer-reviewed papers, making evaluation closer to data-analysis workflows in real papers. SGI-Bench (Xu et al., 2025b) probes scientific general intelligence through scientist-aligned workflows spanning research, idea generation, experimentation, and analysis. AIRS-Bench (Lupidi et al., 2026) and MLR-Bench (Chen et al., 2026) target open-ended AI research or the full research lifecycle, further evaluating problem formulation, experimental progress, and result synthesis in open research settings.
extra_snippets: SciCode (Tian et al., 2024) evaluates code generation for realistic scientific problems, while SciDataCopilot (Rao et al., 2026) focuses on agentic preparation of raw scientific data for discovery workflows. MLAgentBench (Huang et al., 2023) places language agents in machine learning experimentation workflows and evaluates file operations, code execution, and feedback-driven iteration. MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2025) further uses Kaggle competitions to evaluate end-to-end machine learning engineering, and MLGym (Nathani et al., 2025) organizes machine learning research as a gym-style environment emphasizing experimental iteration, result analysis, and strategy adjustment.

extra_snippets: A 2026 evidence review of AI scientists, benchmark gaps, reproducibility limits, and the role human researchers still play. ... In 2025, a manuscript produced by an autonomous research system passed peer review at an ICLR workshop. That milestone shows that an AI scientist pipeline can complete a research cycle.

Completing each stage correctly, consistently, and with evidence that another researcher can inspect is the scientific standard. Those are separate claims. The clearest gap appears on end-to-end evaluations. In Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index science chapter, the leading PaperArena agent scored 38.8%, compared with 83.5% for PhD experts—roughly half the expert score. On ReplicationBench, frontier models completed fewer than 20% of paper-scale astrophysics replication tasks.

Figure 3. An audit trail and controlled execution support reproducibility; scientific validity still depends on review of the evidence and method. The low ReplicationBench result does not prove that one architectural defect explains every failure.

results.title: FIRE-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on the Rediscovery of Scientific Insights
results.description: Our formulation for insight rediscovery is most closely related to reproducibility benchmarks such as PaperBench (Starace et al., 2025), LMR-Bench (Yan et al., 2025), and related efforts (Siegel et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025; Kon et al., 2026), which leverage existing publications as ground truth. These benchmarks evaluate an agent’s ability to replicate reported experiments and results, typically by providing full access to the original paper, including methodology and expected outcomes.
extra_snippets: While this setting is expressive, assessing the scientific validity of generated papers at scale is difficult, and many approaches rely heavily on LLM-based judging as a proxy for expert evaluation (Zheng et al., 2023; Schroeder and Wood-Doughty, 2024; Yin et al., 2026). The second paradigm avoids subjective evaluation of papers by focusing on machine learning tasks with a single performance metric, such as improving model accuracy on a leaderboard (Huang et al., 2024b; Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025). While objective and scalable, these benchmarks often emphasize replication (Starace et al., 2025) and provide limited insight into the broader scientific reasoning process underlying an agent’s behavior.

Our formulation for insight rediscovery is most closely related to reproducibility benchmarks such as PaperBench (Starace et al., 2025), LMR-Bench (Yan et al., 2025), and related efforts (Siegel et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025; Kon et al., 2026), which leverage existing publications as ground truth. These benchmarks evaluate an agent’s ability to replicate reported experiments and results, typically by providing full access to the original paper, including methodology and expected outcomes.

The emergence of autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) holds the promise of accelerating scientific discovery at an unprecedented scale. These “AI researchers” are increasingly capable of automating discrete stages of the research lifecycle, from literature synthesis (Zheng et al., 2025; Schmidgall and Moor, 2025), hypothesis generation (Baek et al., 2025; Si et al., 2025), to coding (Tian et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025), experimentation (Kon et al., 2026), and data analysis (Majumder et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025).

For hypothesis and idea generation, IdeaBench (Guo et al., 2025) and ResearchBench (Liu et al., 2026) focus on the novelty and feasibility of proposed research directions. The execution stage, particularly coding and data analysis, has received the most attention. Benchmarks such as SciCode (Tian et al., 2024) evaluate general scientific programming ability, while BLADE (Gu et al., 2024), DiscoveryBench (Majumder et al., 2025), and ScienceAgentBench (Chen et al., 2025b) emphasize post-hoc data analysis and hypothesis testing.

results.title: stanford-ai-index-2026
results.description: Stanford HAI AI Index Report 2026: science and research findings AI in science is real, measurable, and unevenly distributed — but end-to-end autonomous discovery remains far from reliable.
extra_snippets: Competition-level problem-solving improved sharply — Gemini Deep Think earned a gold medal at IMO 2025 (up from silver in a single year). Rapid gains on FrontierMath and MathArena. Major open problems (long-standing Erdős conjectures) remain well beyond current capabilities. Across every scientific domain, the pattern is consistent: AI performs well on isolated subtasks but struggles when required to execute the multistep workflows that real research demands.

Industry produced over 90% of notable frontier models in 2025, but the most capable models are the least transparent. Training code, parameter counts, dataset sizes, and training duration are no longer disclosed by OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google for their most resource-intensive systems. This creates a structural tension for research institutions relying on these models. As AI is increasingly used in research workflows — from literature synthesis to hypothesis generation — governance frameworks for AI in research are still underdeveloped.
